definition: Doing things in a careful, orderly way, following clear steps one at a time.
example: He took a methodical approach to cleaning the garage, emptying and sorting one shelf before touching the next.
nuance: Methodical stresses following an orderly system; meticulous stresses close attention to tiny details.
prompt: A librarian is searching the building for a rare book that has been misplaced.
options: The methodical librarian checked each shelf in order, beginning with the first aisle.
The methodical librarian pulled books at random from whichever shelf happened to be nearest.
The methodical librarian wrote a long essay comparing the research methods used in libraries.
The methodical librarian glanced around once, shrugged, and declared the book lost forever.
reasons: Working through the shelves in a fixed sequence is an orderly, step-by-step search.
Grabbing books at random is haphazard, the opposite of following a plan.
Writing about methods would be methodological; the word describes how someone works.
A single glance and a quick surrender show no system or patience at all.

practice.prompt: A student has three weeks to prepare for a final exam in chemistry.
options: Her methodical study plan was simply a list of the scientific methods named in her textbook.
Her methodical study plan covered one chapter each evening and ended with a full review.
Her methodical study plan was to skim whatever page fell open the night before the test.
Her methodical study plan switched subjects every hour, depending on her mood at the moment.
reasons: A list about methods confuses the topic with an orderly way of working.
A set schedule that moves chapter by chapter shows steady, organized effort.
Last-minute skimming of random pages has no order or structure.
Choosing topics by whim abandons any consistent system.
